data_quality_assurance:
Collected corpora have been checked and reprocessed for quality and are stored in structured formats such as XML-TEI, XML-OSIS, XML-TEI-EpiDoc, and plain text, depending on the nature of the source. Encoding follows community standards (e.g. TEI P5, OSIS, EpiDoc) with project-specific schema constraints to ensure structural consistency.
Authority files (VIAF, Wikidata) are used systematically for the normalization and disambiguation of named entities.
Data is reviewed and re-encoded by WP8 team members with the collaboration of the PRIN 2022 “Resilient Septuagint” team. Validation is carried out across all formats using schema-aware tools (e.g. oXygen). A versioning system (e.g. Git) is employed to track changes, ensure data integrity, and maintain transparency over time.
An appropriate open and interoperable publication format (e.g. JSON) will be adopted based on uBIQUity platform requirements.
Data is checked and validated by the WP8 team before publication.
dataset.description: Our dataset has been collected, processed, reviewed and/or produced by biblical scholars, patrologists and specialists in Islam of the uBIQUity team, in constant cooperation with IT experts and according to the scientific quality criteria set for ITSERR and RESILIENCE, in machine readable form. Research data enriched with the reference bibliography, templates, training materials and other technical documentation have been saved in a coherent and well-ordered manner in specific shared folders on GDrive and on Zotero, so that they are easier to find, understand and reuse. Regarding biblical texts, the uBIQUity dataset embraces their textual plurality by including some information from the apparatus of their reference editions, which will be made available within the limits posed by copyright.

format: Structured data (HTML, JSON, TEX, XML, RDF)

host.description: Data are stored locally and synchronized with cloud-based repositories (Google Drive and GitHub) to ensure redundancy, version control, and collaborative access. Long-term preservation is guaranteed through deposition in Zenodo, which assigns DOIs and ensures persistent, citable access. All data are saved in open, standard formats (XML-TEI, XML-OSIS, XML-EpiDoc, plain text, JSON), with structured organization in modular folder hierarchies and consistent naming conventions. Metadata is stored either embedded (XML) or in structured files (e.g. JSON, Markdown) and enriched through authority files such as VIAF and Wikidata. Version control is managed through Git, ensuring traceability and integrity of all changes. Data are made openly accessible unless legal, ethical, or copyright constraints require restricted access, in which case appropriate limitations are applied.

host.backup_frequency: Periodic (2 months) backups are made locally, on an external hard drive. Backups are maintained for 2 backup cycles (4 months). At the end of the project, backed up data is deleted, once the primary data (and metadata) is validated.

metadata.description: Metadata in which information protected by copyright is included is not made available, unless proper rights have been explicitly obtained from the copyright holder. Privacy and confidentiality: metadata that contains personally identifiable information related to people who participated in interviews, or to the ITSERR project, or whose personal information has been collected specifically for the ITSERR project, and not as a part of already published material, is not made accessible.

technical_resource.description: The uBIQUity project, which incorporates the “BI” of the Bible(s) and the “QU” of the Qurʾān in its title, investigates the sacred texts of Christianity and Islam in different environments and historical periods through two huge corpora: Greek and Latin Christian commentaries (broadly understood as written forms of exegesis) on the Bible(s) composed from the patristic age until the late Byzantine period, and classical commentaries on the Qurʾān written in Arabic (tafāsīr) from the rise of Islam until the 15th century. Intertextual references, conscious or unconscious, embedded in these ancient works function as invisible “places of memory”, making sacred texts “ubiquitous” (hence the title of the project). Users of uBIQUity software may be researches in different fields of Religious Studies interested in intertextuality within these corpora. They will be able to perform textual queries based on different semantic levels (from identical tokens to contextual similarity), run comparisons, browse texts, take notes, access their workflow, and save previous searches. The software includes various types of data visualization: parallel view, variant graph, distant reading, node-based view. This novel semantic search engine might find further applications in the research of intertextual references in different kinds of literary production.
